question.leadin: You probably know more about Hawaiian mythology than you think you do.
question.text: The menehune (MEN-eh-HOO-neh) are the Hawaiian equivalents of these little people that, in Norse mythology, make excellent smiths.
question.clue: Orange Alternative claimed there could be "no freedom without" what creatures? These creatures were graffitied in spots where Polish authorities had painted over anti-government messages.

swap.leadin: The term "Deluge" refers to a period in which Sweden occupied a union of these two countries, which was governed by a parliament called the sejm (same).
swap.text: Name these two countries that signed the 1569 Union of Lublin, unifying into a commonwealth that would last until it lost its land in a series of 18th century partitions.
swap.answerHtml: Poland and Lithuania [or the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, or Korona Królestwa Polskiego and Didi Kunigystė Lietuvos or the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]
swap.clue: The head of one of these countries instigated Zeligowski's Mutiny in the other.

question.text: This man won the first free Polish election in 1990 after using his leverage as leader of Solidarity to push back Soviet influence at the Roundtable talks.
question.clue: This man mourned his successor in 2010 after that successor died in a Smolensk airport plane crash.

swap.leadin: One of these events in August 1980 was sparked by the firing of Anna Walentynowicz ["VAL-en-TIN-oh-WITCH"].
swap.text: Name this type of action undertaken by workers at the Lenin Shipyards under the leadership of electrical engineer Lech Walesa ["WUH-leh-SUH"]. Arthur Scargill led several of these actions for British coal miners.
swap.answerHtml: strikes [accept labor strikes or strike actions; prompt on protests or walkouts or factory occupations or industrial actions]
swap.clue: The headline "Crisis? What Crisis?" was used to criticize James Callaghan's handling of a wave of these events that became known as the "Winter of Discontent."

question.leadin: It shares Bialowieza Forest with Belarus, home to many big, horned wisents.
question.text: Name this European nation which houses the White Stork Synagogue in Wroclaw, the capital of Lower Silesian Voivodeship. Other cities on the Oder in this country include a town named Police.
question.clue: This country's cavalry never actually attacked tanks with lances at Krojanty during an invasion.

swap.leadin: These events would bring about the end of the Polish Lithuanian Commonwealth.
swap.text: Name these political splittings of Poland Lithuania that took place in the late 18th century. In these events, Prussia, Austria, and Russia invaded and took land, to little resistance.
swap.clue: The three aforementioned treaties dividing Poland are commonly referred to by this term. Another treaty referred to by this term divided British India.

question.leadin: This country united with its neighbor Lithuania under the 1569 Union of Lublin.
question.text: Name this country, whose 1573 Compact of Warsaw guaranteed religious freedom to all free people within its borders.
question.clue: This country was united in the Union of Lublin while it was ruled by the Jagiellonians.

swap.text: This adorable bear was purchased by Polish soldiers during World War II, being taught to move artillery and apparently enjoying eating cigarettes. His name is a diminutive for "joyful warrior."
swap.clue: This Syrian Brown Bear who fought with the Polish II Corps and famously carried 100 pound cases of artillery across the battlefield.

question.leadin: This event was engineered by Frederick the Great in order to avoid the expansion of a Russo-Turkish war.
question.text: Identify this 1772 agreement that enlarged Russia, Prussia, and Austria at the expense of about one-third of another country's territory.
question.answerHtml: the First Partition of Poland [prompt on partial answer]
question.clue: This event was made possible following a victory at Lanckorona by Suvorov over the Confederation of Bar, which had attempted to depose Stanislaw II.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about pre-modern anti-Semitism.
swap.text: In eastern Europe, Jews were confined largely to these autonomous villages within the Pale of Settlement, which were often beset by pogroms.
swap.clue: Eastern European Jews commonly lived in these small, Yiddish-speaking villages found in Poland-Lithuania and, later, the Pale of Settlement.

question.text: Frederick created an elite unit of cavalry of this name, described by the word "totenkopf," or death's head.
question.clue: Jan Sobieski led a decisive charge of these cavalrymen into the Ottoman line during the 1683 Siege of Vienna.

swap.leadin: Twentieth-century Poland went through much turbulence.
swap.text: This former Socialist and editor of the newspaper Robotnik organized the Union of Riflemen to rebel against Russian rule during World War I and ruled newly independent as dictator from 1920 to 1922 and 1926 to 1934.
swap.clue: He ruled from 1918 to 1922 as the head of the military and seized power again in 1926, operating through such proxies as Jozef Beck and trying to appease Hitler until his 1935 death.

question.text: Mieszko conquered this former capital city that contained the Royal Wawel ("VAH-vel") Castle. Supposedly, a creature from this city named Smok Wawelski ("vah-VEL-ski") was tricked to eat sulfur-stuffed cow skins.
question.clue: Casimir III ruled from this city, which eclipsed early royal centers like Plock ("p'wotsk") and Gniezno ("g'nee-EZ-naw") after the pagan king Jogaila was baptized in its cathedral so he could marry the saint Queen Jadwiga ("yahd-VEE-gah").

swap.text: Augustus William of Prussia allegedly died after a broken heart, but really died of a brain tumor, after a crushing defeat in this region. Prussia invaded this region of modern-day Poland to set off the war of Austrian succession.
swap.clue: Frederick the Great's 1740 occupation of this region triggered the War of the Austrian Succession.

question.leadin: Name these periods from medieval Eastern Europe.
question.text: This 1648 to 1667 period in Poland saw large territorial losses to Russia and Sweden; it ended with the abdication of Jan II and the signing of the Truce of Andrusovo.
question.clue: Key precipitating factors of this period include the increased power of the nobility due to Sarmatism and Golden Liberty system, and it saw secondary conflicts like the Second Northern War.

swap.leadin: This house lost power after the death of Casimir III the Great, the son of Wladyslaw the Elbow-High.
swap.text: Name this dynasty founded by Mieszko I that ruled an oft-partitioned country in eastern Europe.

question.text: In Poland, you encounter members of this noble class: they have the power to elect Polish kings, and the liberum veto lets any one of them block a major initiative in the Sejm.
question.clue: Dwor("d'voor") manors were used by this class to manage estates under the folwark ("FOL-vark") system.

swap.text: In 1000 CE, Boleslaw and Otto III of the Holy Roman Empire agreed to establish the first Polish archbishopric at a congress in this Piast capital city, where Saint Adalbert was buried until the corpse was transferred to St. Vitus Cathedral.

question.leadin: Name the following about leaders of Lithuania.
question.text: This Lithuanian prince became King of Poland under the Union of Krewo [krevo] and founded a namesake dynasty that variously ruled Lithuania, Poland, Hungary, and Bohemia.
question.clue: This man concluded the Peace of Thorn after defeating Grandmaster Ulrich von Jungingen (OOL-rick von YOUNG-ing-in) of the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald.

swap.text: This Polish prince converted to Catholicism in order to prevent Polish absorption into the Holy Roman Empire. He also expanded Polish territory to the Baltic Sea.
swap.clue: This ruler who won the battle of Cedynia against Denmark. This father of Sigrid the Haughty may have performed one action to further his alliance with Boleslaw the Cruel.
